segment.source: Connections to storage outside the libraries (Dropbox). The server itself calls the provider, so these are the whole server's settings; Sfe:Locked (connections.*) in the configuration fixes them.
Off: no connection is listed, opened or made, whatever the rights say. Those already made are kept.
One per line. Empty: every kind this server knows.
One per line: account (Only me), library (This space), server (The server).

“Only me” is private to the account that made it, “This space” is shared with a space and its groups, and “The server” is offered to spaces. Connections of a level taken out are kept but can't be used.
The key of the app you registered in Dropbox's App Console. Empty: Dropbox isn't offered.
The app's secret, optional, is set apart and never shown again.
Thumbnails and files of connections kept on this server for previews, for every space. 0 turns it off.
It holds videos being converted, and pictures the provider doesn't make thumbnails of.
A larger file only plays when the browser can play it, and only gets the provider's thumbnail.
What nobody looked at for this long is removed.
Set by the server's configuration: it can't be changed here.
A setting of the whole server: server administrators change it in the server's settings.
Set in each space's own settings.
You don't have the right to change the settings of this section.
Some settings need fixing (see the marked sections).
Ask the server for the settings again
The settings here are only shown in the full view.
Show every setting instead of only the most used ones
Empty the sidebar's “Last searched” and “Last viewed” lists (asks first)
Forgets the searched and viewed tags at once. Tags and files don't change.
Forget the searches this browser suggests again (asks first)
Forgets the searches kept by this browser. Other browsers keep theirs.
Applied without saving, and kept in this browser only: other browsers and devices don't change.
The colours of the pages in this browser, applied at once.
Spaces and users can't change it: the value above applies everywhere.
Users of this space can't change it for themselves.
The bundled fonts are downloaded from this server the first time they are used.
Space between lines, as a multiple of the text size.
The longest a line gets when long lines wrap. About 70 characters is easiest to read.
Space left around the text, on every side.
Long lines continue on the next line instead of going off the side.
Shows the number of each line on the left.

Changes apply as soon as you save them, for everyone using this space (on the server's settings: every space). A setting locked above says why it can't change here. The library's folder, the cache folder, the database, ffmpeg and the server's commands are set in the server's configuration file.
The colours of the pages, in browsers that haven't picked their own below. “Follow the device” uses the light or dark mode of the computer or phone.
How text files read in the viewer, before each browser's own changes (“Aa” in the text's bar).
The colours of the text and of the page behind it.
The name of a font installed on the reader's computer or phone, used where the font is “The font named below”.
Text meant to be read: .txt, .md, README, LICENSE…
Scripts, code, logs, configuration and data files.
Only scripts and other programs using the API ask for pages; the app itself uses the page size above.
Files and folders loaded at a time; more load as you scroll. Smaller pages show up faster on slow drives.
The most items a single request can ask for.
Folders show their first photos and videos: 4 makes a 2×2 grid, 9 a 3×3 grid. 0 lists folders without pictures.
Only the grid and one-per-row views show them, where folders are cards.
Adds buttons that copy the full path of a folder or file on the server.

For example D:\Media\Photos\beach.jpg. The buttons sit next to the location for the current folder, on each folder and file, and in the viewer. Everyone who sees them learns where the library is on the server's disk.
These need the resolutions and durations read by scans (Scanning › Indexing › Read resolutions and durations).
Shows the size in pixels of photos and videos (e.g. 1920×1080) next to their file size, in listings and in the viewer.
Shows how long each video and audio file lasts (e.g. 1:23:45) next to its file size, in listings and in the viewer.
Labels the preview of each photo and video HR (high resolution) or LR (low resolution) in its bottom-right corner, by the thresholds below.
A photo whose shorter side reaches this many pixels is HR.
With 1500, a 2000×1500 photo (or a portrait one of 1500×2000) is HR, and a 1000×1000 one is LR.
A video whose shorter side reaches this many pixels is HR.
With 720, videos of 1280×720 and 1000×1000 are HR, and one of 854×480 is LR. The searches r:hr and r:lr use both thresholds, whether the marks are shown or not.
Search results loaded at a time; more load as you scroll.
The most results a single request can ask for.
Adds a button to the search box that puts the search into words as you type.
It also points out the parts of a search that are ignored, or that don't work the way they may seem to.
The last searches each browser keeps and suggests again as you type, newest first. 0 keeps none.
Each browser keeps its own searches: they never reach the server or other devices.
The Edit button of the viewer crops pictures. The result is saved as a new file, or over the original by those allowed to replace files (its previous version is kept in the trash).
A folder of the library (a path from its top) where edited pictures are saved, in the same folders as their originals. Empty: next to the original.

With Edited, Photos/2024/beach.jpg is saved as Edited/Photos/2024/beach.jpg; the folder is created when first needed. Empty, it is saved as “beach (edited).jpg” next to the original. Existing files are never replaced: a number is added to the name.
How much detail JPEG and WebP pictures keep when saved: higher is sharper and larger.
PNG pictures are saved without loss; other formats are saved as PNG.
Creating folders, renaming, moving, copying, uploading and deleting files and folders from the listing, for the groups given those rights (Spaces & accounts).
Every delete skips the trash: files are gone at once, and only those who may delete permanently can delete.
What is already in the trash stays there.
Items are deleted for good after this many days in the trash. 0 keeps them until the trash is emptied.
A background task does it: Background tasks › Trash purge.
Free space kept by copies and uploads (MB)
A copy or an upload is refused when it would leave less free space than this on the drive it goes to. 0: they may fill the drive.
Larger files are refused before they are sent. 0: no limit (only the free space kept counts).
An upload that receives nothing for this long is removed, with what it received.
Until then, picking the same file again carries on where it stopped.
Downloading several files or a folder makes one zip; a larger one is refused before it starts. 0: no limit.
The size is what the index knows of the files: folders not in the index count for nothing.
New names must also work on Windows. Keep it on when the library is shared with Windows computers or may move to one.
That means no < > : " \ | ? *, no name ending with a dot or a space, and no CON, NUL, COM1… A Windows server always refuses them.
Where SFE keeps its work files
Where the trash and unfinished uploads are kept.

In the library (a hidden .sfe folder at its top), they stay on the library's drive, so moving a file there is instant. In the server's data folder, the library holds nothing of SFE's, but large files are copied from one drive to the other. The name .sfe at the top of the library stays reserved either way.
Find identical files in the library, and keep the tags of files that are moved, renamed, or whose drive was missing during a scan. Both work from the index: scan folders to keep it up to date.
Files with the same size and fingerprint are taken as identical. This needs fingerprints (Scanning › Indexing › Fingerprint files).
Smaller files are left out, as libraries hold many identical tiny files. 0 compares every file.
Groups of identical files loaded at a time; “Load more” shows the next ones.
Adds a Remove button to each copy: the file goes to the trash and its tags are added to a copy you keep.

The two files are compared byte for byte first, so an identical copy always stays. Only groups with the right “Delete duplicates” can remove copies; with “Always delete permanently” (File management), they are deleted for good.
Videos showing the same pictures in other files (another resolution, quality or format, trimmed) are found from fingerprints made with their trickplay: turn trickplay on for the folders to compare.
The share of frames two videos must have in common, out of the longer one. Applies from the next comparison.
A copy at another resolution is near 100%, and a copy cut by a tenth near 90%.
Keep the tags of moved files
A tagged file that a scan no longer finds is remembered with its tags, which move over when it is found again. Off: it loses its tags.
The file is found again when a scan indexes the same file somewhere else: moved, renamed, or back on its drive.
Recognise files without a fingerprint by name
Files indexed without a fingerprint are matched on their name, size and date modified: a move is recognised, a rename is not.
Missing files not found again in that time are forgotten, with their tags. 0: until found or forgotten by hand.
How many tags each section of the sidebar shows.
Records the tags you search for and the tags of the files you open, for the sidebar's “Last searched” and “Last viewed” lists.
Off: nothing new is recorded, and those lists are hidden.
VLC (iPhone, iPad; on a computer only with a vlc:// handler installed)
How far the player's back and forward buttons and the J and L keys jump.
A double tap on the left or right of the picture jumps by the same amount, and each further tap jumps again.
Videos start over when they end. The player's loop button (R) switches it for the video on screen.
The app that the viewer's ▶ button opens videos and audio in, on every browser.
The app must be installed on the device you watch on, and that device must be able to reach this server.
Filled in by the choice above, or written by hand.
{url} is replaced by the file's address, and {encodedUrl} by the same address encoded for a query string. Without either, the address is added at the end (e.g. vlc://).
Shown on its button, as in “Open in VLC”.
How long the link given to the player works, without signing in.
Make it long enough to watch a whole film: players ask again each time you seek. A new password or a disabled account ends the links it gave out.
Flash movies and games (.swf) play in the viewer. Off: .swf files can only be downloaded.
They play through Ruffle, a Flash Player emulator that comes with SFE. A movie can only read the files of its own folder, and never acts as the person watching it.
The http:// or https:// address of another web server that already publishes the library. Files then open from there instead of being streamed by SFE.

The file's path is added after the address, or put where you write {url} (e.g. http://nas/files/{url}?raw=1). {encodedUrl} is the same path fully percent-encoded, slashes too (e.g. http://nas/get?file={encodedUrl}).
These need ffmpeg on the server (System › About says whether it was found). Playback › Video streams lists the videos being converted.
When the browser can't play them
When the browser can't play a video (AVI, WMV, HEVC pictures…), the player asks the server for it converted, from where it was.

Converted videos play as H.264 with AAC sound, which every browser plays. “Always” converts every video, for browsers that play some files without picture or sound. The player's ⟳ button converts the video on screen either way. A conversion keeps the server's processor busy while someone watches.
For the whole server. Each one keeps a processor core or more busy.
Someone asking for one more is told to try again later.
Lower looks better and is heavier: 18 looks like the original, 23 is a good balance, 28 is small.
Taller videos are scaled down to it, keeping their shape (1080 for Full HD). 0 keeps their size.
Pictures already in H.264 (8-bit) are only repackaged, with their sound converted: almost no work for the server.
The catch: a seek lands on the nearest earlier key frame, and the largest height doesn't apply.
Those already made are still shown. “Scans and previews…” in a folder's menu, or Scanning › Excluded folders, adds and removes folders here too.
Shows small pictures of photos and videos, made with ffmpeg and kept in the server's cache folder.
Applies to new thumbnails; existing ones are kept until their file changes.
The moment of a video shown as its thumbnail. Shorter videos use their first frame.
Larger photos are previewed through their thumbnail instead of being downloaded whole. 0 uses thumbnails for every photo.
The viewer shows the thumbnail until the original has loaded.
The one-per-row view shows each photo itself instead of its thumbnail, sharp at any size.
This applies even above the large image size: large photos are downloaded whole as you scroll past them, which can be slow over the network.
Resting the mouse on an animated GIF, PNG, WebP or AVIF plays it (on a touch screen: press and hold).
It concerns animated images shown through their thumbnail. Each time, the whole file is downloaded.
Folders whose files get no new thumbnails, with the folders inside them: paths from the top of the library, one per line.
Thumbnails rendered in parallel. Each one runs ffmpeg, so higher values use more of the processor.
A thumbnail taking longer is given up, and tried again the next time it is asked for.

Trickplay is a strip of small frames taken along a video. The player shows them above its seek bar while you hover over it or drag it, so you can see where you are going. They are made in the background with ffmpeg and kept in the trickplay folder of the server's cache.
The first pass over a large library keeps ffmpeg busy for a long time; later ones only handle new and changed videos.
Folders whose videos get trickplay, with the folders inside them: paths from the top of the library, one per line. Empty: the whole library.
Folders whose videos get no trickplay, with the folders inside them, even inside the folders above.
How often the folders are checked for new videos. 0: no regular check.

The folders are also checked when the server starts and when these settings change, and a video you open is handled right away. Background tasks shows when the next check runs, and can schedule checks at set times.
Resting the mouse on a video plays its trickplay over the thumbnail (on a touch screen: press and hold). Only videos that already have trickplay.
Changing these makes the trickplay of every video again, in the background. The old frames are shown until then.
Time between two frames. Shorter is more precise, but takes longer and more space.
Narrower videos keep their own width.
Frames are stored on sheets of rows × columns.
Bigger sheets mean fewer, larger files.
Decodes only the key frames of each video: many times faster, but a frame can be a few seconds off its position.
Each one runs ffmpeg, which can use several processor cores.
A video taking longer is skipped until it, or these settings, change.
Folder names (not paths) that scans skip, with everything inside them. One per line.
Files of these folders already in the index stay there until the next scan of the folder above them.
File names that scans skip. One per line.
Folders that scans leave out, with the folders inside them: paths from the top of the library, one per line.

What the index already has of them stays as it is, never refreshed. “Scans and previews…” in a folder's menu, or Scanning › Excluded folders, adds and removes them too; ⋮ › Remove from index forgets a folder and can add it here as well.
Includes items marked hidden or system (on Linux and macOS, names starting with a dot), in listings and in scans.
Which files are photos, videos, audio and text, by their extension.
Extensions opened in the photo viewer and given thumbnails, separated by commas.
Extensions played in the video player and given thumbnails and trickplay.
Extensions played in the audio player. Other extensions open in a new tab.
Extensions opened in the text viewer besides those it knows, e.g. dat, out, sub. Not media extensions.
The text viewer already knows .txt, .log, .md, .json, .xml, code and scripts.
Reads the start of each new or changed file to find duplicates and recognise moved files.
It makes scans slower, especially over the network.
Reads the size in pixels of photos and videos, and how long videos and audio last, to show them and search by them (w:, h:, r:, d:).
Files already in the index are read by the next scan. Videos and audio need ffmpeg, which makes scanning new ones slower.
Higher is faster on SSDs and fast network drives; lower is gentler on spinning disks.
Scans, trickplay, similar-video comparisons and thumbnails run in the background. The other tabs show what runs, when each task runs next, the schedules that start them, and the log of every run.
Runs that finished longer ago are forgotten, with their logs. 0: until cleared by hand.
What the server logs (its messages, warnings and errors, for every space) is kept for the Logs page. Both settings are the whole server's.
Older entries are forgotten, and so are the daily files. 0 keeps them forever (the database keeps growing).
Also save the log to files
Writes a copy of every entry to a file per day (sfe-yyyymmdd.log) in the logs folder.
The logs folder is next to the database and the thumbnails (data/logs unless the server's configuration says otherwise). The files are written even while the database can't be.
What SFE does when it is started by hand from its portable package (a double click on Windows, the AppImage on Linux). A service never opens a browser. Both settings are the whole server's.
Opens SFE in this computer's default browser once it is ready.
Starting SFE with --no-browser keeps it closed whatever this says.
Sign the administrator in at once
The browser opened at start signs the server's administrator in without a password. Only for SFE used on this computer alone.
It uses a link that works once, for a minute, from this computer only, and only while the server has a single administrator. Anyone who can start SFE here gets in as the administrator.

A file server drops the connection to a share nobody used for a while (Windows file servers after 15 minutes, many NAS sooner), and the drive may be lost with it. Keep alive looks at the library folder every few minutes, a single read of its first item, so the connection never goes idle. It can't reconnect a drive already lost.
When it is on a network share
“When it is on a network share”: a \\server\share folder, a mapped network drive, or a CIFS, NFS or SSHFS mount, also through a link.
“Always” also pings a folder that SFE can't tell is on the network.
Shorter than the time the file server waits before dropping an idle connection (240: every 4 minutes).
A ping taking longer counts as failed; the next one waits until it ends.
How the library folder is pinged
Write and delete a small file
Reading is enough for most file servers; writing always reaches the server.

The computer may answer a read from its own cache without asking the server. Writing creates and deletes a small file in SFE's work folder (.sfe/keep-alive at the top of the library). When the work folder is on the server (File management), the folder is read instead. More folders are always read.
Folders kept alive too, for those reached through a link to another share: paths from the top of the library, one per line.
“When it is on a network share” looks at each one on its own.
Tokens let programs call the API as the account that made them (My account › Access tokens). These are the whole server's settings.
Off: no token can be made, and those already made are refused. They are kept, and work again once this is back on.
A new token expires after at most this many days. 0 lets a token never expire.
How many tokens an account may hold at once (those neither revoked nor expired).
